title: Verses, Jatakas and Nuns' Songs
bigQuestion: How does the genre of a Buddhist text, whether verse, story or song, change the way it teaches?

story.title: A Song About Gray Hair
story.kicker: An old nun sings about how her body has changed, and why she no longer fears it.
paragraphs: The Therigatha, a collection of poems in the Pali Canon, includes a song credited to a nun named Ambapali. Before she became a nun, the tradition says, Ambapali was a famous and wealthy courtesan of the city of Vesali. She was known for her beauty.

In her song, Ambapali looks at herself in old age. Her hair, she says, was once black and glossy like bees. Now it is rough and white. Her eyes once sparkled like jewels. Now they are dim. The pictures are plain and exact.

Each verse compares then and now. After each comparison comes the same closing line: the words of the one who speaks truth do not change. In the poem, she means the Buddha's teaching that all things change.

Ambapali does not sound bitter. She sounds clear and calm. Buddhist readers have long heard her song as the voice of someone who has seen change deeply and found peace. It is one of the oldest poems credited to a woman anywhere.
story.think: Why might a poem about aging be a powerful way to teach about change?

lessons.title: The Dhammapada
lessons.mainIdea: The Dhammapada is a book of 423 short verses on how to live, grouped into 26 chapters.
reading: The *Dhammapada*, 'verses on the Dhamma', is one of the best-loved Buddhist texts. It has 423 verses in 26 chapters, with titles like 'The Mind', 'Anger' and 'The Fool'. Many Buddhists memorize verses from it.

Each verse is short and easy to remember, often built on a *contrast*: the wise and the foolish, anger and love, a calm mind and a restless one. The first verses begin with the mind as the source of what we do.

Theravada Buddhists teach the Dhammapada to children and quote it in sermons. It has been translated into English many times, starting with Max Müller's version in 1881. Its verses are also read widely beyond Buddhism.

words.d: a Pali book of 423 short verses on how to live, in 26 chapters
setting two different things side by side to show how they differ

look.title: Dhammapada 5
look.text: For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule.
look.cite: Dhammapada, verse 5; tr. F. Max Müller, The Dhammapada, Sacred Books of the East 10 (1881)
look.prompt: What contrast does the verse draw? Why call it 'an old rule'?

check.q: How many verses does the Dhammapada have?
check.why: The Dhammapada has 423 verses in 26 chapters.

check.q: According to Dhammapada 5 (Müller, 1881), how does hatred cease?
check.why: The verse says hatred ceases by love.

check.q: Which basket and collection hold the Dhammapada?
check.why: It is in the minor collection of the Sutta basket.

lessons.title: The Sutta Nipata
lessons.mainIdea: The Sutta Nipata is a collection of verse and mixed talks that many scholars count among the oldest Buddhist texts.
reading: The *Sutta Nipata*, also in the Khuddaka Nikaya, gathers talks mostly in verse. Many scholars think some of its sections, like the Atthakavagga, are among the oldest parts of the Pali Canon, based on their language and style.
It includes the Metta Sutta, on loving-kindness, which is chanted widely in Theravada lands. It also includes the Rhinoceros Sutta, which praises living alone and free, 'like a rhinoceros horn'.

Its verses show an early picture of the wandering monk. Scholars read it for clues about early Buddhist ideals, while Theravada Buddhists chant its verses at blessings and ceremonies. Its central word is *metta*.

words.d: a Pali collection of talks mostly in verse, in the Khuddaka Nikaya
loving-kindness; goodwill toward all beings

look.title: The Metta Sutta
look.text: The sutta describes a wish for all beings, weak or strong, large or small, seen or unseen, near or far, born or yet to be born: may all be happy and at ease. It compares this love to a mother protecting her only child.
look.cite: Sutta Nipata 1.8, Metta Sutta; see V. Fausböll, The Sutta-Nipata, Sacred Books of the East 10, part 2 (1881)
look.prompt: Why might the sutta list so many kinds of beings?

check.q: What does metta mean?
check.why: The Metta Sutta is about loving-kindness.

check.q: Why do many scholars think parts of the Sutta Nipata are very old?
choices: They are carved on Ashoka's pillars
check.why: Scholars date texts partly by language and style.

check.q: In the Metta Sutta, love for all beings is compared to…
choices: A mother protecting her only child
check.why: The sutta uses a mother's love as its image.

lessons.title: Songs of the Elders
lessons.mainIdea: The Theragatha and Therigatha hold poems credited to early monks and nuns about their paths.
reading: Two books in the Khuddaka Nikaya gather poems credited to early disciples. The *Theragatha* holds verses of elder monks. The *Therigatha* holds verses of elder nuns. Each poem is linked to a named person.

The poems are personal. Speakers describe their lives before becoming monks or nuns, their struggles, and the peace they say they found. Some are mothers who lost children; some were servants; some were rich.
Scholars note that the Therigatha is among the oldest collections of women's poetry anywhere. Its *voice* is unusual in ancient literature: women speaking of their own spiritual lives.

words.d: 'verses of the elder nuns', a Pali collection of poems credited to early nuns
'verses of the elder monks', a matching collection for monks
the speaker's personality and point of view in a text

look.title: Two Books of Verse (Approximate)
look.cite: Pali Text Society editions; counts vary by edition
look.prompt: Which collection is larger? What might explain the difference?

check.q: Whose poems are in the Therigatha?
check.why: Theri means elder nun.

check.q: Why do scholars find the Therigatha remarkable?
choices: It is the longest Buddhist book
It is among the oldest collections of women's poetry
check.why: Women's voices from that age are rare.

check.q: What does 'voice' mean in a poem?
choices: The speaker's personality and point of view
check.why: The Therigatha's voices are personal and distinct.

lessons.title: How a Jataka Is Built
lessons.mainIdea: A Jataka has a story in the present, a story of the past, and a link showing who was who.
reading: The *Jataka* collection holds 547 stories of the Buddha's past lives, as Buddhists tell them. In each, the future Buddha, called the *Bodhisatta*, appears as a human, animal or god.

Each Jataka has three parts. First comes a story in the present: something happens among the Buddha's monks. Then the Buddha tells a story of the past. Last comes the link, naming who each character was reborn as, such as 'the monkey king was I'.

The verses inside each Jataka are counted as canonical. The prose stories around them come from a later commentary. This is why scholars speak of *layers* in the text. Scholars date the commentary to around the 5th century CE.

words.d: a story of one of the Buddha's past lives; there are 547 in the Pali collection
Pali for the future Buddha in his past lives (Sanskrit: bodhisattva)
parts of a text added at different times

look.title: The Monkey King's Bridge
look.text: In the Great Monkey Jataka, the Bodhisatta is a monkey king who stretches his body across a river as a bridge so his troop can flee the archers. A king watching is moved by his sacrifice.
look.cite: Mahakapi Jataka (Jataka no. 407); The Jataka, ed. E.B. Cowell, vol. 3, tr. H.T. Francis and R.A. Neil (1897)
look.prompt: Which of the three parts of a Jataka is this? What value does it teach?

check.q: How many Jatakas are in the Pali collection?
check.why: The Pali Jataka has 547 stories.

check.q: What comes last in a Jataka?
choices: The link naming who each character was
check.why: The link connects past characters to present people.

check.q: Which part of the Jataka is counted as canonical?
check.why: The prose comes from a later commentary.

lessons.title: Jatakas in Art and Life
lessons.mainIdea: Jataka stories are carved, painted, performed and retold across Buddhist Asia.
reading: Jataka stories appear on the gateways of Sanchi, the walls of Borobudur and the painted caves of Ajanta in India. Artists showed several scenes of one story in a single panel. Visitors still walk past these panels today.
In Thailand, Laos and Myanmar, the last ten Jatakas, called the Ten Great Births, are especially loved. The last, the Vessantara Jataka, is performed or recited at a yearly festival in some places.

In the Vessantara Jataka, Prince Vessantara gives away everything, even his wife and children. Many Buddhists see it as a picture of perfect *generosity*. Some Buddhist listeners have found it painful and ask hard questions about it. The story ends with the family reunited.

words.d: the last and longest Jataka, about a prince famous for giving
giving freely; one of the perfections in Buddhist teaching

look.title: Two Readers of Vessantara
look.text: A Thai monk says: Vessantara shows the highest giving, and the story ends with the family together. A student says: I feel for the children, who had no choice. Both are reading the same Jataka.
look.prompt: How can both responses be honest ways of reading the story?

check.q: Where can you see Jataka carvings?
check.why: Jatakas are carved on many Buddhist monuments.

check.q: What does Prince Vessantara give away?
choices: Everything, even his wife and children
check.why: The story tells of his complete giving.

check.q: How do Buddhist listeners respond to the Vessantara Jataka?
choices: Many praise its generosity, and some find it painful
It is only read in America
check.why: Responses vary among Buddhists.

lessons.title: The Cowell Translation
lessons.mainIdea: The first complete English Jataka, edited by E.B. Cowell (1895–1907), is now in the public domain.
reading: Between 1895 and 1907, Cambridge scholar E.B. Cowell edited *The Jataka, or Stories of the Buddha's Former Births* in six volumes. Several translators shared the work, including Robert Chalmers, W.H.D. Rouse, H.T. Francis, R.A. Neil and E.J. Thomas.

This was the first complete English Jataka. It is now in the public domain. In 1916, Francis and Thomas published a shorter selection called *Jataka Tales* for general readers. Many school libraries still hold it.

Like other translations of its time, the English is formal and sometimes old-fashioned. Modern scholars check it against the Pali. Still, it remains a key source for students who want to read the tales in full.

words.d: a particular published version of a text
a person who puts a text into another language

look.title: The Cowell Jataka
look.cite: The Jataka, ed. E.B. Cowell, Cambridge University Press (1895–1907)
look.prompt: How many years did the full translation take?

check.q: Who edited the first complete English Jataka?
check.why: Cowell edited the six volumes (1895–1907).

check.q: What was Jataka Tales (1916)?
choices: A shorter selection for general readers
check.why: Francis and Thomas selected tales for a wider audience.

check.q: Why can students quote the Cowell translation freely?
choices: It was written by the Buddha

check.why: Its copyright has expired.

lessons.title: Buddhaghosa the Commentator
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhaghosa, a 5th-century scholar in Sri Lanka, wrote commentaries that shape how Theravada reads the Canon.
reading: *Buddhaghosa* was an Indian monk who came to Sri Lanka in the 5th century CE, tradition says. At the Great Monastery in Anuradhapura, he studied old commentaries written in Sinhala.

He put these commentaries into Pali. His best-known work, the *Visuddhimagga* or 'Path of Purification', is a large guide to Theravada teaching and practice. Many commentaries on the suttas are credited to him.

A *commentary* explains a text, word by word or story by story. For many Theravada Buddhists, reading the Canon means reading it through Buddhaghosa. Modern scholars sometimes compare his readings with the older texts.

words.d: a 5th-century CE monk-scholar in Sri Lanka who wrote major Pali commentaries
a text that explains another text
'Path of Purification', Buddhaghosa's large guide to Theravada teaching

look.title: Text and Commentary
look.text: A verse says: the mind is hard to guard, quick and flits wherever it wants. A commentary adds a story of a monk who could not settle his mind until the Buddha gave him advice. The story helps readers picture the verse.
look.prompt: What does the commentary add? What might it change?

check.q: Where did Buddhaghosa do his work?
check.why: He worked at the Great Monastery in Anuradhapura.

check.q: What is the Visuddhimagga?
check.why: Its title means Path of Purification.

check.q: What is a commentary?
choices: A text that explains another text
check.why: Commentaries explain words and stories in scripture.

lessons.title: Why Genre Matters
lessons.mainIdea: The genre of a text, whether rule, talk, list, verse or story, tells readers how to read it.
reading: A *genre* is a kind of writing with its own shape and purpose. The Pali Canon holds many genres: rules in the Vinaya, talks in the suttas, lists in the Abhidhamma, verses in the Dhammapada, songs in the Therigatha, stories in the Jatakas.
Each genre works differently. A rule tells what to do. A talk explains and argues. A verse sticks in memory. A story builds feelings and shows values in action. A song gives a personal voice.
Knowing the genre helps a reader ask the right questions. You would not read the Therigatha like a rulebook, or the Vinaya like a poem. Scholars call this paying attention to *form*.

words.d: a kind of writing with its own shape and purpose
the shape of a text, such as verse, story or list

look.title: Genres in the Pali Canon
look.cite: Standard counts for the Pali Canon
look.prompt: Match each number to its genre: verse, story, rule or list.

check.q: What is a genre?
choices: A kind of writing with its own shape and purpose
check.why: Rules, talks, verses and stories are different genres.

check.q: Which genre does the Vinaya mainly hold?
check.why: The Vinaya is the rulebook of monastic life.

check.q: Why does genre matter to a reader?
choices: It tells the reader the price
It helps the reader ask the right questions
check.why: Different forms call for different kinds of reading.

lessons.title: One Teaching, Many Forms
lessons.mainIdea: The same Buddhist idea can appear as a talk, a verse, a story and a song.
reading: Take the teaching of *impermanence*, the idea that all things change. In a sutta, the Buddha, as the text presents him, argues it step by step. In the Dhammapada, a short verse states it memorably.

In a Jataka, a character learns it through events. In the Therigatha, Ambapali sings it as she looks at her aging body. Each form reaches readers in a different way. Ambapali uses the same idea in her song.

Buddhist teachers have long used many forms to reach many kinds of people. Scholars of religion see this range of genres as one reason these texts have lasted. They call a text's intended readers its *audience*.

words.d: the Buddhist teaching that all things change (Pali: anicca)
the people a text is written or told for

look.title: Four Ways to Say It
look.text: Talk: the Buddha asks if body and feeling are permanent. Verse: a Dhammapada line compares the body to a bubble or a mirage. Story: a Jataka king sees a gray hair and leaves his throne. Song: Ambapali compares her youth and age.
look.prompt: Which form do you find most powerful? Why?

check.q: What is impermanence?
choices: The teaching that all things change
check.why: Impermanence (anicca) is a core Buddhist teaching.

check.q: In which text does Ambapali sing about aging?
check.why: Her poem is in the Therigatha.

check.q: Why do scholars think many genres helped these texts last?
choices: Long texts are easier to carry
They were all written in one year
check.why: A range of forms reaches many kinds of audiences.

lessons.title: The Makhadeva Story
lessons.mainIdea: In one Jataka, a king sees his first gray hair and decides to leave the throne for a religious life.
reading: In the Makhadeva Jataka, a long-lived king tells his barber to warn him when he sees a gray hair. One day the barber finds one and pulls it out. He waits many years before the barber finds one. The king then calls his son to him.
Looking at the gray hair, the king feels that death has come near. He hands his kingdom to his son and leaves to live as an ascetic. The tale's final link names the Bodhisatta as King Makhadeva.

Buddhist teachers use this story to talk about change and priorities. Readers notice how it matches Ambapali's song: both use gray hair as a sign of impermanence. Here, one *image* connects two genres, story and song, and becomes a *motif*.

words.d: a picture in words that a reader can imagine
an image or idea that appears again and again in stories

look.title: The First Gray Hair
look.text: The king tells his barber to report the first gray hair. When it appears, he takes it in his hand and says that his days are passing. He gives the kingdom to his eldest son and goes forth.
look.cite: Makhadeva Jataka (Jataka no. 9); The Jataka, ed. E.B. Cowell, vol. 1, tr. Robert Chalmers (1895)
look.prompt: Why does a single gray hair change the king's life?

check.q: What makes King Makhadeva leave his throne?
choices: A dream of a white elephant
check.why: The gray hair reminds him that life passes.

check.q: What image connects the Makhadeva Jataka and Ambapali's song?
check.why: Both use gray hair as a sign of change.

check.q: What is a motif?
choices: An image or idea that appears again and again
check.why: Gray hair is a motif across Buddhist texts.
